title: Mobile-First 3D Board Game — Touch Interaction & Runtime Spec (phone browser, link-opened)
rules: Ship one non-scrolling stage: `position:fixed` body, `overscroll-behavior:none`, `touch-action:none` on the canvas. Because the document never scrolls, the address bar never auto-collapses, so `100svh` and `100dvh` are identical at runtime — size the stage in `svh` so a later scrollable overlay (rules sheet) can never trigger a canvas resize.

Use `viewport-fit=cover` and floor every safe-area inset: `max(env(safe-area-inset-bottom), 12px)`. Android Chrome reports 0 for insets despite a 24dp gesture bar, so a raw `env()` puts your control bar on the back-gesture strip.
Let the WebGL canvas bleed edge-to-edge behind the insets; apply insets only to the HUD layer. The board should touch the bezel; the buttons must not.

Kill double-tap zoom with `touch-action:manipulation` on DOM controls and `touch-action:none` on the canvas — not with `user-scalable=no`, which iOS Safari ignores. Add `preventDefault` on `gesturestart/gesturechange/gestureend` to stop iOS page-pinch.
Bind canvas interaction to Pointer Events only (`pointerdown/move/up/cancel` + `setPointerCapture`). Never mix touch and mouse listeners — you will double-fire on hybrid devices.
Keep DOM buttons on `click`, not `touchstart`. With `touch-action:manipulation` the 300ms delay is already gone, and `click` preserves keyboard, switch-control and screen-reader activation.
Decide gesture intent exactly once, at the moment travel first exceeds 10 CSS px, and never revisit it for that gesture. Re-deciding mid-drag is what makes 3D boards feel drunk.

Reserve one-finger drag for orbit, two-finger drag for pan, two-finger distance for dolly. Do not put pan on one finger — on a 390px-wide screen users cannot reliably distinguish their own orbit from their own pan.
Only let a one-finger drag become a piece drag when `pointerdown` raycast-hit a piece the player is legally allowed to move; otherwise it is always orbit.
Tap = pointer up within 250 ms and under 10 px total travel. Long-press = 500 ms under 10 px. Anything else is a drag.
When a finger lifts out of a two-finger gesture, enter a `settle` state and ignore the remaining pointer until all pointers are up. Otherwise the camera snaps violently as pinch hands over to orbit.

Primary controls live in a bottom bar centred at y≈770 on 390×844 and y≈744 on 360×800 — inside the right-thumb comfort arc. Destructive actions (resign, new game) go deliberately in the top-right hard-reach zone behind a 44px icon.

Minimum hit target 48×48 CSS px, 56px tall for primary actions, 12px minimum gap between adjacent targets. 44px (≈11.6 mm) is the Apple floor; a finger contact patch is 8–10 mm with ±2 mm centroid error, so 48px buys the margin that stops mis-taps at the edge of the bar.
Cap the bottom bar at 4 targets on a 360px viewport (4×64 + 3×12 = 292px inside 328px usable). A fifth control goes into an overflow sheet, never squeezed.
Keep all horizontal drag surfaces at least 20px from the left and right screen edges — iOS back-swipe and Android back-gesture own those strips and you will never win them.

Render on demand. A turn-based board should draw 0 frames while the player is thinking: `invalidate()` on camera change, tween tick or state change, then stop after 2 quiet frames. This is the single largest battery and thermal lever available.

Prefer `antialias:true` with a pixel-ratio clamp of 1.5 over `antialias:false` at DPR 2. Mobile tile-based GPUs (Mali, Adreno, Apple) resolve 4× MSAA in tile memory almost free, whereas every extra fragment is paid in full.
Budget the whole scene at ≤60 draw calls, ≤45,000 triangles, ≤8 materials, ≤6 textures at ≤1024², ≤24 MB texture VRAM. Use one `InstancedMesh` per piece type.
Bake board ambient occlusion into the board albedo and run one 1024² directional shadow map with `shadowMap.autoUpdate = false`, flipping `needsUpdate` only on frames where pieces actually move.
Ban post-processing entirely. One full-screen pass on a 390×844 at DPR 2 is ~1.3 M fragments before you have drawn anything.

Detect thermal throttling from a rolling EMA of frame time: step quality down after 2 s above 22 ms, and only step back up after 30 s below 13 ms. Downgrade DPR first, then shadow resolution, then shadows, then AA.

Never call `screen.orientation.lock()` and never show a 'please rotate your device' screen. Refit the camera on orientation change by taking the tighter of the horizontal and vertical FOV, and animate the refit over 250 ms.

In portrait, offset the projection upward by ~6% of viewport height with `camera.setViewOffset` so the board centre clears the thumb bar; in landscape, move controls to a vertical stack on the right edge.

Paint something in under 100 ms: inline critical CSS, a solid `theme-color`, the board silhouette, and the opponent's name parsed synchronously from the share link. Never a white flash, never a bare spinner.
Create the `AudioContext` lazily inside the first `pointerup`, and default sound to OFF for a link-opened session — someone opening a shared link is often in public.

Request zero permissions on load: no geolocation, notifications, motion, clipboard, fullscreen or install prompt in the first session. Request `navigator.wakeLock` only after the first interaction, and release it on `visibilitychange`.

Meet 4.5:1 for text and 3:1 for board graphics and UI components, and never encode player identity in colour alone — pair the blue/amber palette with distinct piece silhouettes and a glyph on legal-move markers.

Because you have suppressed browser pinch-zoom, you owe the user an in-game text-scale toggle (100/115/130%) driven by a `--ui-scale` multiplier on rem-based sizes. Do not set `html { font-size }` in px — that destroys the user's own browser font setting.

Honour `prefers-reduced-motion` in both CSS and the animation system: camera fly-ins become instant cuts, dice tumbles become a 200 ms cross-fade to the result, idle camera drift is disabled outright.
Mirror board state into a hidden DOM grid with `role="grid"` and announce turns via a terse `aria-live="polite"` region. A `<canvas>` is invisible to assistive technology.
antiPatterns: `height: 100vh` on the stage — on iOS this is the *large* viewport height, so the bottom 60–90px of your UI sits under the address bar on first paint.

Reaching for `100dvh` reflexively: on a non-scrolling game it is identical to `svh`, and on any page that *can* scroll it makes the canvas resize continuously as the bar animates — a full renderer and framebuffer reallocation per frame.
`user-scalable=no` / `maximum-scale=1` as the double-tap-zoom fix. iOS Safari ignores both for accessibility reasons; only `touch-action` actually works.
`document.addEventListener('touchmove', e => e.preventDefault())` on the whole document — it kills every scrollable overlay you will later add (rules, settings, chat) and makes the page feel broken.
Mapping one-finger drag to pan and requiring two fingers to orbit. Users grip a phone one-handed; the default single-finger gesture must be the one they use constantly.
Deciding orbit-vs-drag from the *current* frame's movement vector rather than latching it at the 10px threshold — produces jitter where a piece drag intermittently orbits the camera.
Reading `e.movementX` on touch pointers. Support is inconsistent across Safari versions; store the previous position per `pointerId` and compute the delta yourself.
Handing over from pinch to orbit the instant one finger lifts, causing a camera snap of hundreds of pixels.
`PCFSoftShadowMap` plus multiple shadow-casting lights. It is roughly double the cost of `PCFShadowMap` for a difference nobody sees at 390px wide.
`renderer.setPixelRatio(window.devicePixelRatio)` unclamped — DPR 3 on a 393×852 screen is 3.0 M fragments per full-screen draw and will thermally throttle a mid-range phone within ninety seconds.
A `requestAnimationFrame` loop that renders every frame for a turn-based game. It drains battery, heats the device, and buys nothing between moves.
`EffectComposer` with bloom or SSAO 'just for the board glow'. Fake it with an emissive material and a baked glow texture.
Leaving `ACESFilmicToneMapping` on for the low tier — measurable per-fragment cost for a look the player never compares against.
Listening to `window.resize` for canvas sizing. Use `ResizeObserver` on the container; `resize` fires on every keyboard open and address-bar twitch.
Forcing landscape, or showing a rotate-your-phone interstitial. It breaks orientation-lock users and reads as an unfinished port.
Autoplaying a theme tune, or constructing the `AudioContext` at module load — iOS starts it suspended, logs warnings, and can hard-block later playback.
A modal tutorial, cookie banner, or 'add to home screen' prompt in the first three seconds of a link-opened session. Each one is a measurable bounce.
Red-vs-green player colours, and legal-move highlights that are colour-only with no glyph.
Buttons under 44px, or a 56px button with a 4px gap to its neighbour — the gap matters as much as the size.
Binding game actions to `touchstart` on DOM buttons for 'responsiveness'. It fires during scroll intent, cannot be cancelled by sliding off, and is invisible to switch control.
notes:
Test matrix that actually catches these bugs: (1) a real iPhone on Safari — the iOS Simulator does not reproduce thermal throttling, safe-area behaviour under `black-translucent`, or the pinch-to-orbit handover; (2) a Snapdragon 6-class or Mali-G57 Android on Chrome for the quality-tier step-down; (3) Chrome DevTools at 4x CPU throttle plus Fast 4G for the first-three-seconds budget; (4) iOS Safari with Reduce Motion and Larger Text both enabled. Instrument `renderer.info.render.calls` and the frame-time EMA behind a `?dev=1` flag so the budgets in section 10 are observable in the field rather than merely asserted in a document.

Two decisions worth confirming before build. First, dolly-versus-pan on two fingers: this spec drives both simultaneously from the same gesture (distance to dolly, centroid to pan), which matches every map application and is what users expect. The alternative — gating on whichever delta dominates in the first 20px — is more precise but feels sticky on a 390px screen, and I would not ship it. Second, the `low` tier drops real-time shadows in favour of instanced blob decals. That is a visible art change, not just a resolution change, so the blob decal must be authored alongside the real shadow from the outset rather than bolted on when the first slow device turns up.

The two highest-leverage items if scope has to be cut: render-on-demand (section 8) and the intent latch at the 10px threshold (section 6). The first is worth more battery and thermal headroom than every other optimisation combined for a turn-based game; the second is the difference between a camera that feels solid and one that feels haunted.
